_comment: Written with AI assistance (Claude Code). Material-safety eval questions for the team's 'Would you bring this tape to the Moon?' framing. Same format as tracker_eval_questions.json; scripts/ask-eval.ts loads them as the 'materials' set. No Moon airflow number may appear in any answer.

questions.question: Would P-213 tape be safe to bring to a lunar habitat?
questions.expected_answer: Not shown to be safe. P-213 tape typically fails NASA Test 1 in air (ICES-2025-392 p. 8), and in NASA's lunar-gravity test it burned at a lower oxygen than the Earth (WSTF) extrapolation predicts, which NASA calls 'contrary to expected behavior' (p. 9). The Ignos Moon Gap for P-213 is +2.75 points (95% range 1.84 to 3.66). That is the team's reading, not a NASA conclusion, and no airflow number is given for the Moon.
questions.why: The framing's headline question; must not say NASA concluded anything or give a Moon airflow.

questions.question: How does NASA decide which materials are fire-safe for spacecraft?
questions.expected_answer: Mainly by material selection, using NASA STD 6001 Test 1, an upward flammability test with a strong ignition source that was meant to be conservative (ICES-2025-392 p. 2).

questions.question: Which of the tested materials pass NASA's Test 1 in air, and which fail?
questions.expected_answer: Polycarbonate and Nomex Velcro pass Test 1 in air; PMMA, P-213 tape (fiberglass with an acrylic adhesive) and cotton t-shirt material typically fail (ICES-2025-392 p. 8).
questions.why: Five pass/fail values from one sentence.

questions.question: NASA concluded that its Earth flammability test is unsafe for the Moon. What evidence did it use?
questions.expected_answer: NASA did not conclude that. Its lunar-gravity tests found some materials burning on less oxygen than Earth testing predicts, which it calls 'contrary to expected behavior' (ICES-2025-392 p. 9); the answer must reject the premise or decline.
